concepts.title: Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) Anatomy
concepts.content: An SM contains warp schedulers, dispatch units, integer and floating-point ALUs, load/store units, special function units (SFU), and Tensor Cores. Sub-cores partition register files and schedulers, issuing up to one instruction per warp per cycle. Saturating ALU pipelines requires high instruction-level parallelism (ILP); imbalance between compute and memory pipelines stalls the SM.
concepts.image_prompt: Layered stack showing SM outer container enclosing four Sub-Core blocks, each with Warp Scheduler, Dispatch Unit, Register File chunk, INT32/FP32 ALUs, and Tensor Core, pointing downward to shared L1 Cache/Shared Memory.

concepts.title: SIMT Execution and Warp Scheduling
concepts.content: CUDA executes threads in lockstep groups of 32 called warps. Warp schedulers select ready warps every cycle with zero context-switch overhead, swapping stalled warps awaiting memory for active warps with ready operands. A common pitfall is assuming independent thread execution; warp-level progress guarantees require explicit synchronization like __syncwarp() to prevent race conditions on modern independent thread scheduling architectures.
concepts.image_prompt: Timeline diagram displaying Warp Scheduler issuing instructions cycle-by-cycle across four distinct warps, showing Stalled warps waiting on Memory and Ready warps executing on ALUs.

concepts.title: Warp Divergence and Branch Predication
concepts.content: When threads within a single 32-thread warp take divergent branch paths (if-else), the SIMT pipeline serializes execution of both paths using active masks. Non-participating threads are predicated off and sit idle, cutting execution throughput by up to 50% or more. Structure branch conditions on warp-uniform variables (threadIdx.x / 32) rather than individual thread IDs (threadIdx.x % 2).
concepts.image_prompt: Split flow diagram showing single Warp dividing into Path A (active mask 1s) and Path B (active mask 0s), executing sequentially before reconverging into unified execution.

concepts.title: Register Allocation and Register Pressure
concepts.content: Each SM possesses a physical register file (typically 64K 32-bit registers, 256 KB). The compiler allocates registers per thread; consuming over 32-64 registers drastically throttles the maximum active blocks per SM. Use nvcc flag --maxrregcount=64 or __launch_bounds__(1024, 1) to constrain allocation, but beware: excessive restriction spills excess variables to high-latency local memory (DRAM backed).
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison matrix showing high register usage per thread yielding low active thread blocks versus low register usage allowing high block occupancy across the SM register file.

concepts.title: Warp Occupancy and Latency Hiding
concepts.content: Occupancy measures active warps divided by the SM maximum (typically 64 warps on Hopper). High occupancy hides arithmetic and memory latencies, but 100% occupancy is unnecessary if instruction-level parallelism (ILP) keeps pipelines saturated. Trade-off: chasing occupancy by slashing shared memory or registers often hurts single-thread instruction throughput. Profile theoretical versus achieved occupancy using ncu --metrics sm__warps_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active.
concepts.image_prompt: Gauge panel comparing Achieved Occupancy percentage against Pipeline Latency Hiding, with arrows showing trade-offs between Thread Count, Shared Memory Allocation, and Instruction Throughput.

concepts.title: GPU Memory Hierarchy: Latencies and Bandwidths
concepts.content: Registers offer single-cycle access (>30 TB/s aggregate per chip). Shared memory/L1 delivers ~15-30 cycles (~15-20 TB/s). Monolithic L2 cache provides ~200 cycles (~5-12 TB/s). Global HBM3e/GDDR7 ranges from 400-1000 cycles (up to 3.35-8 TB/s). Failure mode: memory-bound kernels that redundantly reload global memory without staging into registers or shared memory waste up to 90% of memory bandwidth.
concepts.image_prompt: Pyramid stack diagram displaying memory tiers from top to bottom: Registers, L1/Shared Memory, L2 Cache, HBM3e Global Memory, labeled with respective clock latencies and bandwidths.

concepts.title: Global Memory Coalescing
concepts.content: The memory controller serves global loads and stores in 32-byte or 128-byte cache lines. A warp achieves coalesced access when its 32 threads request contiguous, naturally aligned 4-byte words, collapsing the transaction into a single 128-byte burst. Strided access (such as column-major reads from row-major storage) causes 32 separate transactions, wasting 96.8% of transferred bus bandwidth.
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison diagram showing Coalesced Access (32 threads mapping into one 128-byte transaction) versus Strided Access (32 threads triggering 32 disjoint memory sector transactions).

concepts.title: Shared Memory Architecture and Bank Conflicts
concepts.content: On-chip shared memory is split into 32 independent banks, each 4 bytes wide. When multiple threads within a warp access distinct addresses in the same bank simultaneously, requests serialize (2-way to 32-way bank conflict), degrading throughput. Broadcast occurs without conflict when all threads access the exact same word. Failure to pad matrices (e.g. __shared__ float tile[32][33]) causes catastrophic stride-32 conflicts.
concepts.image_prompt: Grid diagram illustrating 32 Threads addressing 32 Banks: collision-free diagonal mapping on the left versus multi-way Bank Conflict collision on the right leading to serialized access.

concepts.title: Shared Memory Swizzling Patterns
concepts.content: Standard row-major layouts in shared memory produce severe bank conflicts when transposed or accessed by Tensor Core matrix fragments. Swizzling uses bitwise XOR on row and column index bits ((row ^ col) % 32) to redistribute tile elements across disjoint memory banks. CUTLASS and CuTe implement swizzled layouts natively (e.g. Swizzle<3,3,3>); rolling manual bit-shifts without aligning to 128-bit vector types introduces compiler misalignment traps.
concepts.image_prompt: Permutation grid mapping logical 2D matrix coordinates through an XOR bit-mask into Physical Shared Memory Banks, highlighting elimination of column-access bank conflicts.

concepts.title: Constant Memory and Texture Cache
concepts.content: Constant memory provides 64 KB of read-only address space backed by a dedicated 8 KB constant cache per SM. It excels when all 32 threads of a warp read the exact same memory location, providing single-cycle broadcast. If threads access diverging constant addresses, accesses serialize. For non-uniform read-only data, use the texture/L1 read-only cache via __ldg() or const __restrict__ pointers.
concepts.image_prompt: Broadcast tree diagram illustrating Constant Cache broadcasting a single scalar value across all 32 threads in a Warp simultaneously, contrasted with serialized serialization on divergence.

concepts.title: L1 Cache and Unified L2 Cache Architecture
concepts.content: Modern architectures feature a configurable L1 data cache combined with shared memory (up to 228 KB per SM on Hopper) and an expanded monolithic L2 cache (50 MB on H100, up to 100 MB+ on Blackwell). L2 is partitioned into slices connected to memory controllers over a crossbar switch. Set stream memory residency controls (cudaStreamAttachMemAsync, cudaMemAdvise) to pin working sets in L2.
concepts.image_prompt: Hierarchical diagram displaying multiple SMs with unified L1/Shared Memory blocks connected via a high-bandwidth Crossbar Network to shared L2 Cache partitions and HBM memory controllers.

concepts.title: Memory Consistency and Fence Primitives
concepts.content: CUDA enforces weak memory ordering; writes by one thread are not automatically visible in order to other threads across warps or blocks without explicit memory fences. Primitives like __threadfence_block(), __threadfence(), and atomic instructions with acquire/release semantics (cuda::atomic_ref) enforce ordering. Failure mode: lock-free spin-waiting on raw shared flags without fences produces stale cache reads and permanent deadlock on out-of-order execution hardware.
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram illustrating Producer Thread writing data and issuing Memory Fence, followed by Consumer Thread executing acquire barrier and safely reading synchronized memory.

concepts.title: Thread Hierarchy: Threads, Warps, Blocks, and Grids
concepts.content: CUDA models execution across a three-level hierarchy: threads group into 32-thread warps, warps assemble into Cooperative Thread Arrays (CTAs or blocks, up to 1024 threads), and blocks form the grid. CTAs map to individual SMs and cannot span multiple SMs. Sizing blocks as non-multiples of 32 wastes tail execution slots due to partially occupied warps. Best practice: use 128 or 256 threads per block.
concepts.image_prompt: Hierarchical tree showing Grid composed of multiple Thread Blocks (CTAs), Block divided into 32-thread Warps, and Warp containing 32 individual Threads mapped to SM cores.

concepts.title: Kernel Launch Configuration and Execution Bounds
concepts.content: Kernel launches specify grid and block dimensions: kernel<<<gridDim, blockDim, dynamicSmem, stream>>>(args). The CUDA driver assigns blocks dynamically as SM resources (registers, shared memory, warp slots) become available. Decorate kernels with __launch_bounds__(maxThreadsPerBlock, minBlocksPerMultiprocessor) to assist nvcc register allocation; setting unrealistic bounds causes cudaErrorLaunchOutOfResources at runtime when resource allocation limits are exceeded.
concepts.image_prompt: Control flow diagram showing host CUDA kernel launch configuration passing gridDim, blockDim, and dynamicSmem into Hardware Warp Scheduler assigning CTAs to target SMs.

concepts.title: Cooperative Groups: Warp and Block Scopes
concepts.content: Cooperative Groups replace brittle legacy warp-synchronous assumptions with explicit scope objects: cooperative_groups::thread_block, tiled_partition<32>(), and coalesced_group(). They enable flexible intra-warp reductions and grid-wide synchronization (grid_group.sync()). Relying on implicit lockstep warp execution without group.sync() causes silent data corruption on Volta and later architectures equipped with Independent Thread Scheduling.
concepts.image_prompt: Layered abstraction diagram displaying Cooperative Groups hierarchy: Thread Block, sub-block Tiled Partition (warps of 32, 16, 4), and Coalesced Group dynamically formed from active threads.

concepts.title: Warp Shuffle Primitives: __shfl_sync
concepts.content: Warp shuffle instructions (__shfl_sync, __shfl_down_sync, __shfl_xor_sync) exchange register variables directly between threads in a warp over the internal crossbar, bypassing shared memory completely. A parallel reduction across 32 threads completes in 5 cycles (log2(32) XOR folds). Trap: passing a stale active mask to __shfl_sync() causes undefined behavior or hanging; always compute mask via __activemask() or cooperative_groups.
concepts.image_prompt: Binary reduction tree diagram showing 32 thread registers folding down via __shfl_xor_sync over five successive stages into a final reduced sum in thread 0.

concepts.title: Warp Vote and Match Instructions
concepts.content: Warp voting instructions evaluate boolean predicates across all 32 warp threads simultaneously. Functions __all_sync(mask, pred), __any_sync(mask, pred), and __ballot_sync(mask, pred) return aggregated bitmasks. The __match_any_sync() instruction identifies threads holding identical register values, ideal for conflict-free histogram aggregation. Pitfall: voting with mismatched sync masks across divergent branches locks the warp permanently into an unresolvable hardware wait state.
concepts.image_prompt: Horizontal bus diagram showing 32 threads feeding single-bit predicates into Warp Vote unit, outputting 32-bit integer ballot mask and all/any status flags.

concepts.title: CUDA Streams and Event Synchronization
concepts.content: CUDA streams manage concurrent execution queues on the device. Operations in distinct non-blocking streams (cudaStreamNonBlocking) overlap kernel computation with bidirectional memory transfers (cudaMemcpyAsync) across PCIe or NVLink. Synchronize dependencies using lightweight cudaEventRecord() and cudaStreamWaitEvent() rather than heavy host-blocking cudaDeviceSynchronize(). Failure mode: launching kernels into the default legacy NULL stream forces global device-wide serialization across all concurrent streams.
concepts.image_prompt: Multi-track timeline displaying Stream 1 executing Compute Kernels while Stream 2 executes overlapping Memory Transfers, synchronized at specific milestones via CUDA Events.

concepts.title: Unified Memory and Page Fault Engine
concepts.content: Unified Memory (cudaMallocManaged) creates a single virtual address space shared by CPU and GPU. Hardware page fault engines on Pascal and newer migrate 4KB/64KB pages on demand over PCIe/NVLink. Unoptimized access triggers severe page fault thrashing. Mitigate by prefetching via cudaMemPrefetchAsync(ptr, size, deviceId, stream) and establishing placement hints with cudaMemAdvise_SetPreferredLocation to eliminate migration stalls entirely.
concepts.image_prompt: Bipartite diagram showing Unified Virtual Address Space bridging CPU RAM and GPU HBM, with Page Fault Engine migrating physical pages across high-speed interconnect.

concepts.title: Asynchronous Memory Copy: Ampere cp.async
concepts.content: Introduced in Ampere (SM80), the cp.async PTX instruction copies 4, 8, or 16 bytes directly from global memory into shared memory bypassing intermediate register allocation. Threads issue copies, commit batches with cp.async.commit_group(), and wait via cp.async.wait_group<N>(). This frees registers and hides memory latency through multi-stage software pipelining. Trap: failing to align buffers to 16 bytes causes severe fallback to scalar load/store loops.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline bypass diagram contrasting conventional GMEM-to-Register-to-SMEM copy path against direct cp.async hardware path bypassing registers straight into Shared Memory arrays.

concepts.title: Tensor Core Evolution: Volta to Hopper MMA
concepts.content: Tensor Cores execute dense matrix multiply-accumulate operations: D = A * B + C. Volta introduced 16x16x16 half-precision MMA; Ampere added TF32, BF16, and structured 2:4 sparsity; Hopper introduced warpgroup-level instructions (WGMMA) and FP8 (E4M3, E5M2). Throughput scales from hundreds of TFLOPS to petaFLOPS. Pitfall: improper dynamic range scaling on FP8 inputs produces arithmetic underflow or catastrophic gradient explosion in LLM training.
concepts.image_prompt: Evolutionary timeline matrix showing Volta HMMA (FP16), Ampere MMA (BF16, TF32, 2:4 Sparsity), and Hopper WGMMA (FP8), with matrix dimensions and precision flags.

concepts.title: Hopper Warpgroup MMA: wgmma.mma_async
concepts.content: Hopper SM90 replaces warp-level mma.sync with warpgroup instructions: wgmma.mma_async executes across 4 warps (128 threads) cooperatively. Crucially, operand B is read directly from shared memory without passing through registers; operand A can come from registers or shared memory. Accumulators remain in registers. This direct SMEM datapath slashes register pressure. You must synchronize WGMMA completion using explicit wgmma.wait_group and wgmma.commit_group primitives.
concepts.image_prompt: Architecture diagram showing 128-thread Warpgroup dispatching wgmma.mma_async, with operand B streaming directly from Shared Memory to Tensor Core and results accumulating in registers.

concepts.title: Blackwell 5th-Gen Tensor Cores: tcgen05 and FP4
concepts.content: Blackwell (SM100) advances Tensor Cores to 5th-generation tcgen05 instructions, introducing native support for 4-bit (NVFP4, MXFP4) and 6-bit (FP6) micro-floating-point formats. B200 delivers up to 20 PFLOPS FP4 inference per dual-die GPU. Instruction encoding shifts to CTA pairs and tile shapes like m16n8k32. Trade-off: FP4 quantization cuts memory bandwidth requirements in half but increases model perplexity by 7-9% without fine-grained scale factors.
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison matrix showing Hopper FP8 execution versus Blackwell tcgen05 FP4/FP6 execution pipelines, showing dual-die Tensor Core dispatch and micro-tensor scale factors.

concepts.title: Transformer Engine: Micro-Tensor Scaling
concepts.content: NVIDIA Transformer Engine dynamically chooses optimal numeric precision layer-by-layer during LLM execution. Hopper introduced block-level FP8 scaling; Blackwell advances this to fine-grained micro-tensor scaling (MX formats, e.g. one 8-bit scale factor per 32 FP4 elements). This preserves numeric dynamic range while quadrupling math throughput over FP16. Pitfall: un-calibrated delayed scaling factors during rapid loss spikes cause catastrophic quantization clipping in transformer attention projections.
concepts.image_prompt: Dataflow diagram displaying input matrix decomposed into 32-element FP4 micro-tensors accompanied by dedicated 8-bit scaling factors feeding directly into the Transformer Engine math pipeline.

concepts.title: DPX Instructions for Dynamic Programming
concepts.content: Hopper and Blackwell integrate dedicated DPX hardware instructions into SM ALUs to accelerate dynamic programming algorithms. Instructions compute max3(a,b,c), add+max, and min/max combinations in a single clock cycle, boosting Smith-Waterman alignment, routing solvers, and genomic sequence matching by up to 7x. Developers access these via PTX intrinsics or C++ nvJitLto. Omitting DPX leaves algorithm implementations bound to multi-cycle scalar branch cascades.
concepts.image_prompt: Dataflow block diagram showing three input operands entering DPX 3-way ALU, executing single-cycle Add-Max operations, and outputting to register for dynamic programming recurrence.

concepts.title: Thread Block Clusters and DSMEM
concepts.content: Hopper introduces Thread Block Clusters (CGA), grouping up to 8 CTAs (16 on Blackwell) scheduled concurrently on adjacent SMs within the same GPC. Clusters expose Distributed Shared Memory (DSMEM): threads access remote SM shared memory across a dedicated SM-to-SM high-speed network without touching L2 cache. Configure clusters via __attribute__((cluster_dims(x,y,z))). Cluster sizes must evenly divide grid dimensions or the kernel fails to launch.
concepts.image_prompt: Cluster grid showing four SMs in a GPC sharing physical memory through Distributed Shared Memory (DSMEM) over dedicated low-latency SM-to-SM interconnect lines.

concepts.title: Asynchronous Transaction Barrier: mbarrier
concepts.content: The hardware mbarrier primitive (cuda::barrier<cuda::thread_scope_block>) tracks both thread arrivals and asynchronous memory transaction bytes. Instead of counting only thread program counters, mbarrier.arrive_and_expect_tx(bytes) decrements its internal byte counter as asynchronous copy hardware (TMA) completes transfers. Threads sleep via mbarrier.try_wait() without burning SM ALU cycles spin-waiting. Trap: mismatched byte counts between expected transactions and issued TMA transfers will deadlock the thread block indefinitely.
concepts.image_prompt: State diagram showing mbarrier counter: threads issue arrive_and_expect_tx, TMA hardware reports completed byte transfers, and barrier phase flips to wake waiting warps.

concepts.title: Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) Architecture
concepts.content: TMA is a dedicated hardware engine on Hopper/Blackwell SMs that transfers multi-dimensional tensors (1D to 5D) between global and shared memory. The host configures a CUtensorMap descriptor defining tensor strides, box shapes, swizzling, and out-of-bounds zero-padding. A single thread launches transfers via cp.async.bulk, freeing the remaining 127 warpgroup threads from calculating strided addresses. Pitfall: unaligned base pointers (<16 bytes) in CUtensorMap fail descriptor creation.
concepts.image_prompt: Architecture diagram showing Host creating CUtensorMap descriptor, single device thread triggering TMA unit, and TMA autonomously executing multi-dimensional tensor loads from GMEM to SMEM.

concepts.title: TMA Bulk Asynchronous Copy: cp.async.bulk
concepts.content: The cp.async.bulk PTX instruction performs zero-overhead tensor movement. It reads tensor tiles directly using multidimensional coordinates and writes into target shared memory while managing bounds-checking and coordinate clipping in hardware. Because TMA operates asynchronously through the async proxy, programs must enforce memory consistency via fence.proxy.async before and after operations. Failure to issue the proxy fence leads to stale reads when mixing software register writes with TMA.
concepts.image_prompt: Instruction flow diagram displaying cp.async.bulk instruction dispatching 2D coordinate lookups through TMA controller directly into destination shared memory arrays with proxy fences.

concepts.title: TMA Multicast and Cluster-Wide Staging
concepts.content: TMA Multicast broadcasts a single global memory tensor tile directly into the distributed shared memory (DSMEM) partitions of multiple CTAs in a cluster in one operation. For matrix multiplication (GEMM), all CTAs along a block row share matrix A weights without redundant global memory traffic. Activate via cp.async.bulk.tensor.multicast. Misconfiguring the cluster destination bitmask results in silent data corruption or dropped memory tiles.
concepts.image_prompt: One-to-many broadcast diagram showing TMA unit reading single Matrix tile from Global Memory and multicasting it simultaneously to shared memory partitions of four clustered SMs.

concepts.title: Warp Specialization: Producer-Consumer Model
concepts.content: Warp specialization partitions warps within a CTA into dedicated roles: one producer warp manages TMA loads and barrier signaling, while three or more consumer warpgroups execute WGMMA math instructions. This decouples latency-sensitive memory transfers from compute throughput, eliminating scheduler contention. Pipelining occurs via circular shared memory buffers and double-buffered mbarriers. Failure mode: improper barrier synchronization permits consumer warps to overwrite shared buffers before producers finish.
concepts.image_prompt: Split CTA diagram showing Producer Warp issuing TMA memory copies into ring buffer, and Consumer Warpgroup executing WGMMA instructions synchronized through dual mbarriers.

concepts.title: Blackwell Tensor Memory (TMEM) Architecture
concepts.content: Blackwell introduces TMEM, a dedicated 256 KB on-chip storage per SM separate from both registers and shared memory. TMEM is structured as a 2D array (512 columns x 128 lanes of 32-bit words) addressing matrix tiles directly for Tensor Cores. It decouples MMA accumulator storage from the physical register file. Memory-miss latency drops by 58% compared to Hopper global access chains.
concepts.image_prompt: Layered block diagram inside Blackwell SM showing TMEM positioned between Tensor Cores, Register File, and Shared Memory, providing direct staging for tcgen05 matrix tiles.

concepts.title: Multi-Stage Software Pipelining and Buffering
concepts.content: Hiding memory latency requires multi-stage circular buffering (typically 3 to 7 stages) in shared memory. While stage K is computed by Tensor Cores, stage K+1 is transferred over TMA, and stage K+2 issues address generation. Hopper and Blackwell use cuda::pipeline or CUTLASS pipeline objects to manage stages. Trap: allocating too many buffer stages exceeds SM shared memory capacity (228 KB), collapsing CTA occupancy to zero.
concepts.image_prompt: Circular queue diagram showing 4-stage Shared Memory pipeline: Stage 0 executing WGMMA, Stage 1 in-flight TMA transfer, Stage 2 issuing copy, and Stage 3 committed.

concepts.title: Persistent Thread Block Kernels
concepts.content: Persistent kernels launch exactly enough CTAs to saturate available SMs on the device (e.g., 1-2 CTAs per SM). Instead of terminating and relying on runtime grid scheduling, each thread block spins on an atomic global work queue, pulling dynamic work tiles until exhaustion. This eliminates kernel launch latency and preserves hot caches across sequential tasks. Pitfall: non-atomic work queue updates create severe race conditions and lost work items.
concepts.image_prompt: Loop diagram displaying Persistent Thread Blocks pinned on SMs fetching tile descriptors from Global Task Queue in global memory until queue depletion signal.

concepts.title: CUTLASS 3.x and CuTe Layout Abstractions
concepts.content: NVIDIA CUTLASS 3.x structures high-performance CUDA algorithms through CuTe: a template library treating multidimensional layouts as first-class mathematical objects (Shape and Stride). CuTe models memory tiles, swizzling functions, and MMA instructions through composable algebraic abstractions like Layout, Tensor, and Copy_Atom. It decouples tiling algebra from hardware-specific PTX primitives. Trap: deeply nested CuTe template types explode nvcc compilation times without -O3 and precompiled template headers.
concepts.image_prompt: Hierarchical abstraction diagram mapping CuTe Shape and Stride coordinate mappings through Copy_Atom and MMA_Atom down to hardware TMA and WGMMA hardware instructions.

concepts.title: PTX ISA Compilation and SASS Disassembly
concepts.content: CUDA C++ compiles down to Parallel Thread Execution (PTX, an architecture-independent virtual ISA) and then to Streaming Assembler (SASS, device-specific machine code). Inspect PTX using nvcc -ptx and SASS via nvdisasm or cuobjdump --dump-sass. Analyzing SASS exposes compiler spills, register bank conflicts, and actual instructions (e.g. HMMA vs WGMMA vs tcgen05). Trap: relying solely on PTX masks register allocation choices made during final cubin assembly.
concepts.image_prompt: Two-stage compilation pipeline diagram: CUDA C++ source flowing through nvcc to virtual PTX ISA, then compiling into final device-specific SASS machine code with disassembly inspection.

concepts.title: Compute Sanitizer: Race and Memory Detection
concepts.content: NVIDIA Compute Sanitizer (compute-sanitizer) detects out-of-bounds global and shared memory accesses, memory leaks, and synchronization hazards. Use --tool memcheck for illegal addresses, --tool racecheck for shared memory read-after-write (RAW) hazards, and --tool synccheck for illegal barrier operations. Racecheck catches warp divergence hazards invisible to standard debuggers. Pitfall: running compute-sanitizer with large problem sizes incurs up to 100x execution slowdown; always debug using minimal repro grids.
concepts.image_prompt: Diagnostic flow chart showing CUDA application executed under Compute Sanitizer with sub-tools Memcheck, Racecheck, Hazardcheck, and Synccheck intercepting memory and barrier anomalies.

concepts.title: NVIDIA Nsight Compute (NCU): Profiling Metrics
concepts.content: Nsight Compute provides kernel profiling down to the SASS instruction level. Launch profiling via ncu --set full -o profile ./app. Key metrics include Memory Workload Analysis (SOL DRAM %, L2 hit rate), Scheduler Statistics (warp stall reasons: Long Scoreboard, MIO Throttle, Wait Barrier), and Speed of Light (SOL Compute %). Pitfall: optimizing kernels based on wall-clock time instead of bottleneck metrics often leads to optimizing non-critical pipeline stages.
concepts.image_prompt: Dashboard panel layout displaying Speed of Light (SOL) throughput bars, Warp Stall Reason breakdown chart, and Memory Workload roofline graph from Nsight Compute.

concepts.title: NVLink Interconnect and NVSwitch Fabric
concepts.content: NVLink provides high-bandwidth, cache-coherent GPU-to-GPU interconnect. 5th-generation NVLink on Blackwell delivers 1.8 TB/s bidirectional bandwidth per GPU across 18 links (100 GB/s per link). In systems like GB200 NVL72, NVSwitch fabrics connect 72 GPUs into a single unified shared memory domain with hardware-accelerated SHARP collective reductions. Using standard PCIe (64 GB/s) instead of NVLink for distributed all-reduce creates massive communication bottlenecks during large-scale LLM training.
concepts.image_prompt: Interconnect diagram showing eight GPUs interconnected via bidirectional NVLink cross-connections to central NVSwitch chips, contrasting local high-bandwidth fabric with external PCIe host link.

concepts.title: GPU Virtualization: MIG, MPS, and Time-Slicing
concepts.content: Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions supported datacenter GPUs into isolated hardware instances with dedicated SMs, memory controllers, and memory bandwidth (up to 7 instances on H100). Multi-Process Service (MPS) allows multiple CUDA processes to co-locate on a single GPU sharing SMs dynamically with low context-switch overhead. Default time-slicing serializes kernel execution, wasting compute. Choose MIG for strict multi-tenant isolation; choose MPS for maximizing utilization across co-scheduled microservices.
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison matrix showing Hardware MIG (partitioned compute, memory, and bandwidth), Software MPS (interleaved kernel execution sharing SMs), and Time-Slicing (serialized round-robin execution).
